To improve upon our earlier approximation, we compute the Green’s function to second order in $1/g$ . At this order, we obtain the following result:

$$ \displaystyle\overline{\lambda} \displaystyle=\frac{g^{2}}{4}+\frac{9}{4}, \displaystyle Q_{r}(\omega_{n}) \displaystyle=\frac{g}{\omega_{n}^{2}(1+3/g^{2})+(\overline{\lambda}-3)}, \displaystyle\Sigma_{r}(\tau) \displaystyle=\frac{3g^{5}}{2(g^{4}-9)}e^{-g|\tau|\sqrt{\frac{g^{2}-3}{g^{2}+3}}}, \displaystyle\Sigma_{r}(\omega_{n}) \displaystyle=\frac{3g^{6}}{\sqrt{g^{4}-9}}\frac{1}{g^{2}(g^{2}-3)+\omega_{n}^{2}(g^{2}+3)}. $$

We therefore conclude that at large $g$ , the spectral function has the form of a delta function

$$ \displaystyle\rho(\omega)=\frac{g^{3}}{g^{2}+3}\delta\left(\omega^{2}-\frac{g^{2}}{4}\frac{g^{2}-3}{g^{2}+3}\right), $$

with a finite gap. Thus, within this approximate framework, we expect the replica-symmetric solution to persist up to $g\approx\sqrt{3}$ .

## Appendix E Replica identities

We consider $n\times n$ replica matrices $A_{ab}$ whose off-diagonal elements are parametrized by the Parisi function $a(u)$ , $u\in[0,1]$ , and the diagonal element $A_{aa}=\tilde{a}$ (similarly for $B_{ab}$ and $C_{ab}$ ). We find it useful to define

$$ \displaystyle\langle a\rangle\equiv\int_{0}^{1}du\,a(u),\, $$

and

$$ \displaystyle[a](u)\equiv-\int_{0}^{u}dva(v)+ua(u)\,. $$

For the replica-symmetric case, we take

$$ \displaystyle a(u)=a,\quad\quad\tilde{a}=a+\sigma_{a}\,. $$

For the case of one-step replica symmetry breaking, we take

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{a} \displaystyle=a_{1}+\sigma_{a}, \displaystyle a(u) \displaystyle=\begin{cases}a_{1}\,,\quad\mbox{$x<u<1$}\\
a_{0}\,,\quad\mbox{$0<u<x$}\end{cases}. $$

Then, we have $\langle a\rangle=a_{1}-x(a_{1}-a_{0})$ , and

$$ \displaystyle[a](u)=\begin{cases}x(a_{1}-a_{0})\,,\quad&\mbox{$x<u<1$}\\
0\,,\quad&\mbox{$0<u<x$}\end{cases}. $$

We now present some useful identities for matrix operations in the limit $n\rightarrow 0$ .

### E.1 Term-by-term sum

$$ \frac{1}{n}\sum_{a,b=1}^{n}A_{ab}=\tilde{a}-\langle a\rangle. $$

### E.2 Matrix product

For

$$ C_{ab}=\sum_{c=1}^{n}A_{ac}B_{cb}\,, $$

we have [72]

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{c} \displaystyle=\tilde{a}\tilde{b}-\langle ab\rangle, \displaystyle c(u) \displaystyle=(\tilde{b}-\langle b\rangle)a(u)+(\tilde{a}-\langle a\rangle)b(u)-\int_{0}^{u}dv(a(u)-a(v))(b(u)-b(v)). $$

### E.3 Matrix inverse

To determine $B=A^{-1}$ , we set $C=1$ in the matrix product to obtain the relations

$$ \displaystyle 1 \displaystyle=\tilde{a}\tilde{b}-\langle ab\rangle, \displaystyle 0 \displaystyle=(\tilde{b}-\langle b\rangle)a(u)+(\tilde{a}-\langle a\rangle)b(u)-\int_{0}^{u}dv(a(u)-a(v))(b(u)-b(v)). $$

With replica-symmetric matrices, we have

$$ \displaystyle\sigma_{b} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sigma_{a}}, \displaystyle b \displaystyle=-\frac{a}{\sigma_{a}^{2}}. $$

For the case of one-step replica symmetry breaking, we have

$$ \displaystyle 1 \displaystyle=\tilde{a}\tilde{b}-a_{0}b_{0}x-a_{1}b_{1}(1-x), \displaystyle 0 \displaystyle=(\tilde{b}-b_{0}x-b_{1}(1-x))a_{0}+(\tilde{a}-a_{0}x-a_{1}(1-x))b_{0}, \displaystyle 0 \displaystyle=(\tilde{b}-b_{0}x-b_{1}(1-x))a_{1}+(\tilde{a}-a_{0}x-a_{1}(1-x))b_{1}-x(a_{1}-a_{0})(b_{1}-b_{0}). $$

Solving these equations, we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\sigma_{b} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sigma_{a}}, \displaystyle b_{1} \displaystyle=-\frac{a_{1}\sigma_{a}+x(a_{1}-a_{0})^{2}}{\sigma_{a}(\sigma_{a}+x(a_{1}-a_{0}))^{2}}, \displaystyle b_{0} \displaystyle=-\frac{a_{0}}{(\sigma_{a}+x(a_{1}-a_{0}))^{2}}. $$

### E.4 Term-by-term inverse sum

If $A^{-1}=B$ , then from (204)

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\sum_{ab}A^{-1}_{ab}=\tilde{b}-\langle b\rangle. $$

From (207), we have

$$ \displaystyle 1 \displaystyle=\tilde{a}\tilde{b}-\langle ab\rangle, \displaystyle 0 \displaystyle=(\tilde{b}-\langle b\rangle)\langle a\rangle+(\tilde{a}-\langle a\rangle)\langle b\rangle-\langle ab\rangle+\langle a\rangle\langle b\rangle. $$

Taking the difference, we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\sum_{ab}A^{-1}_{ab}=\frac{1}{\tilde{a}-\langle a\rangle}. $$

### E.5 Term-by-term product

For the product

$$ D_{ab}=\sum_{c,d=1}^{n}A_{ac}B_{db}\,, $$

we use the fact that $\sum_{c}A_{ac}$ is independent of the index $a$ for replica matrices. This yields a replica-symmetric matrix $D_{ab}$ , which is of independent $a,b$ and using (204) we have

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{d}=d(u)=(\tilde{a}-\langle a\rangle)(\tilde{b}-\langle b\rangle). $$

For the replica-symmetric case, $\tilde{d}=d=\sigma_{a}\sigma_{b}$ , and $\sigma_{d}=0$ . With one-step replica symmetry breaking $\tilde{d}=d_{0}=d_{1}=(\sigma_{a}+x(a_{1}-a_{0}))(\sigma_{b}+x(b_{1}-b_{0}))$ , and $\sigma_{d}=0$ .

### E.6 Trace log

The trace log is needed in the computation of the free energy. We have [72]

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\mbox{Tr}\ln A=\ln(\tilde{a}-\langle a\rangle)+\frac{a(0)}{\tilde{a}-\langle a\rangle}-\int_{0}^{1}\frac{du}{u^{2}}\ln\frac{\tilde{a}-\langle a\rangle-[a](u)}{\tilde{a}-\langle a\rangle}\,. $$

In the replica-symmetric case, we have

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\mbox{Tr}\ln A=\ln(\sigma_{a})+\frac{a}{\sigma_{a}}\,. $$

With one-step replica symmetry breaking, we have

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\mbox{Tr}\ln A=\ln(\sigma_{a})+\frac{a_{0}}{\sigma_{a}+x(a_{1}-a_{0})}-\frac{1}{x}\ln\frac{\sigma_{a}}{\sigma_{a}+x(a_{1}-a_{0})}\,. $$

Let us now consider $\mbox{Tr}\ln(A+B)$ , where $B$ is a constant matrix, i.e., $\tilde{b}=b(u)=b$ , and $\sigma_{b}=0$ . Then, we have

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\mbox{Tr}\ln(A+B)=\frac{1}{n}\mbox{Tr}\ln A+\frac{b}{\tilde{a}-\langle a\rangle}. $$

### E.7 Cubic term

According to (3.72) in Ref. 48, for the matrix $q_{ab}$ with $\tilde{q}=0$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\mbox{Tr}q^{3}=\int_{0}^{1}du\left[u[q(u)]^{3}+3q(u)\int_{0}^{u}dv[q(v)]^{2}\right]. $$

# On $1/N$ diagrammatics in the SYK model beyond the conformal limit

**Authors:** \firstnameIrina \lastnameAref’eva\fnsep ††thanks: Email: arefeva@mi.ras.ru Affiliation: Steklov Mathematical Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences, Gubkina str. 8, 119991, Moscow, Russia \firstnameMikhail \lastnameKhramtsov\fnsep ††thanks: Email: khramtsov@mi.ras.ru Affiliation: Steklov Mathematical Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences, Gubkina str. 8, 119991, Moscow, Russia \firstnameMaria \lastnameTikhanovskaya\fnsep ††thanks: Email: tikhanovskaya@mi.ras.ru Affiliation: Steklov Mathematical Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences, Gubkina str. 8, 119991, Moscow, Russia

## Abstract

In the present work we discuss aspects of the $1/N$ expansion in the SYK model, formulated in terms of the semiclassical expansion of the bilocal field path integral. We derive cutting rules, which are applicable for all planar vertices in the bilocal field diagrams. We show that these cutting rules lead to novel identities on higher-point correlators, which could be used to constrain their form beyond the solvable conformal limit. We also demonstrate how the cutting rules can simplify the computation of amplitudes on an example of the six-point function.

## 1 Introduction and summary of results

The SYK model [1, 2, 3, 4] is a maximally chaotic quantum mechanical many-body model that is solvable at large $N$ . It also displays emergent conformal symmetry in the strong coupling limit, that is broken both spontaneously and explicitly. Maximal chaos and emergent conformal symmetry at strong coupling motivate using the SYK model as a holographic toy model for quantum near-extremal black holes [2, 6, 5].

The SYK is a model of $N$ interacting Majorana fermions, living in $(0+1)$ (Euclidean) dimensions. The Hamiltonian is given by [2]:

$$ H=\frac{1}{4!}\sum_{ijkl}j_{ijkl}\chi_{i}\chi_{j}\chi_{k}\chi_{l}\, $$

The couplings $j_{ijkl}$ are randomized with respect to the Gaussian distribution $P(j_{ijkl})=\sqrt{\frac{N^{3}}{12\pi J^{2}}}\ \mathrm{e}^{-\frac{N^{3}j_{ijkl}^{2}}{12J^{2}}}$ . The correlation functions and other physical quantities in the model are supposed to be disorder-averaged, using the rules

$$ \langle j_{ijkl}\rangle=0\,,\qquad\langle j_{ijkl}^{2}\rangle=\frac{3!J^{2}}{N^{3}} $$

At finite temperature the constant $\beta J$ admits the role of the dimensionless coupling; in the IR limit the model is in the strong coupling regime $\beta J\gg 1$ . At large $N$ limit in the language of Feynman diagrams in terms of Majorana fermions all correlation functions of the model are dominated by the melonic graphs and their cuts [2, 7, 8].

An alternative formulation of the model can be obtained by averaging over the disorder in the partition function, introducing colorless bilocal auxiliary fields $\tilde{G}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})$ and $\tilde{\Sigma}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})$ and integrating out the fermions (see [4] for detailed derivation):

$$ Z=\int D\tilde{G}D\tilde{\Sigma}\ \mathrm{e}^{-S[\tilde{G},\tilde{\Sigma}]}\,; $$

where the action in terms of $G$ , $\Sigma$ fields has the form:

$$ S[\tilde{G},\tilde{\Sigma}]=-\frac{N}{2}\text{Tr}\log(\partial_{\tau}-\hat{\tilde{\Sigma}})+\frac{N}{2}\int d\tau d\tau^{\prime}\left(\tilde{\Sigma}(\tau,\tau^{\prime})\tilde{G}(\tau,\tau^{\prime})-\frac{J^{2}}{4}\tilde{G}(\tau,\tau^{\prime})^{4}\right)\,, $$

(here and henceforth the notation $\hat{F}$ means the integral operator with the kernel $F(\tau,\tau^{\prime})$ ). This path integral describes accurately describes the first few orders in $1/N$ , where the replica-diagonal assumption is valid11 1 The replica-nondiagonal saddle points of the disorder-averaged free energy are discussed in [13, 14, 15].. The factor $N$ in the action justifies the usage of the steepest descent method to evaluate the path integral at large $N$ . Thus the large $N$ expansion of SYK in terms of the bilocal fields is a semiclassical expansion for the path integral (3). The fermionic correlators of the SYK model are expressed in terms of the correlators of the field $\tilde{G}$ :

$$ \langle\chi_{i_{1}}(\tau_{1})\chi_{i_{2}}(\tau_{2})\dots\chi_{i_{2n-1}}(\tau_{2n-1})\chi_{i_{2n}}(\tau_{2n})\rangle=\langle\tilde{G}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})\dots\tilde{G}(\tau_{2n-1},\tau_{2n})\rangle\,. $$

In the strong coupling limit $\partial_{\tau}\to 0$ the action (4) is conformally invariant. The conformal parts of all correlation functions in SYK can be computed analytically [2, 3, 8], however on the level of $4-$ and higher-point functions there are contributions that break the conformal symmetry and dominate in the $\beta J\to\infty$ limit. The non-conformal contributions come from the reparametrization soft mode [3, 11, 9, 4, 10], which is dual to the gravitational mode in the bulk theory. Because of this, the studies of the non-conformal corrections to the correlation functions in SYK can be useful to gain insight into the full bulk dual of SYK.

In this work we discuss the technical tools which could be used to perform such calculations. Our main result are the cutting rules for planar diagrams. These cutting rules are exact in $\beta J$ , and can be applied at any order of the $1/N$ expansion to either obtain additional constraints on the higher-point correlators beyond the conformal limit, or to simplify the calculations, as we demonstrate on the example of the non-conformal six-point function.

## 2 Systematic $1/N$ expansion in SYK

Suppose $G$ , $\Sigma$ is the large $N$ saddle point of the path integral (3). We define new variables

$$ g=|G|(\tilde{G}-G)\,,\quad\sigma=\frac{1}{J^{2}|G|}(\tilde{\Sigma}-\Sigma)\,, $$

and perform the semiclassical expansion in the bilocal fluctuation fields $g$ , $\sigma$ . The action (4) in terms of these fluctuation fields reads

$$ \displaystyle S[g,{\sigma}] \displaystyle= \displaystyle S_{0}[G,\Sigma]-\frac{N}{2}\text{Tr}\log(1-J^{2}\hat{G}\circ\widehat{\sigma|G|}) \displaystyle+ \displaystyle\frac{NJ^{2}}{2}\int d\tau d\tau^{\prime}\left(\sigma g+|G|G\sigma-\frac{1}{4}g^{4}{1\over|G|^{4}}-g^{3}{G\over|G|^{3}}-\frac{3}{2}g^{2}{G^{2}\over|G|^{2}}\right)\,. $$

We consider the diagrammatics for this action. Every propagator of a bilocal field carries a factor of $1/N$ , whereas every vertex carries a factor of $N$ . Therefore, the degree of a bilocal graph, contributing to a correlator, in the $1/N$ expansion is given by

$$ \deg=L-V $$

where $L$ is the amount of lines in the diagram and $V$ is the number of vertices.

### 2.1 Propagators

The two-point functions of the bilocal fields are determined by the quadratic part of the action (7) [3]:

$$ \displaystyle S^{(2)}=-\frac{NJ^{2}}{12}\int d^{4}\tau\ \sigma(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})\tilde{K}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2},\tau_{3},\tau_{4})\sigma(\tau_{3},\tau_{4}) \displaystyle+\frac{NJ^{2}}{2}\int d\tau_{1}d\tau_{2}\left[g(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})\sigma(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})-\frac{3}{2}g(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})^{2}\right]\,. $$

Here $\tilde{K}$ is the symmetric ladder kernel [3]:

$$ \tilde{K}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2},\tau_{3},\tau_{4})=-3J^{2}|G(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})|G(\tau_{1},\tau_{3})G(\tau_{2},\tau_{4})|G(\tau_{1},\tau_{4})| $$

Inverting the quadratic form, we find the propagators:

$$ \displaystyle\langle g(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})g(\tau_{3},\tau_{4})\rangle=\frac{2}{3NJ^{2}}\left(\frac{\tilde{K}}{1-\tilde{K}}\right)(\tau_{1},\tau_{2};\tau_{3},\tau_{4})\,; \displaystyle\langle g(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})\sigma(\tau_{3},\tau_{4})\rangle=\frac{2}{NJ^{2}}\left(\frac{1}{\tilde{K}-1}\right)(\tau_{1},\tau_{2};\tau_{3},\tau_{4})\,; \displaystyle\langle\sigma(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})\sigma(\tau_{3},\tau_{4})\rangle=\frac{6}{NJ^{2}}\left(\frac{1}{\tilde{K}-1}\right)(\tau_{1},\tau_{2};\tau_{3},\tau_{4})\,. $$

The geometric series of the inverse ladder kernel in (11) is precisely the sum of the ladder diagrams, contributing to the fermionic four-point function. It can be computed explicitly by diagonalizing the ladder kernel in the conformal limit [2, 3, 11]. Schematically, one obtains

$$ \langle g\ g\rangle=\mathcal{F}_{\text{non-conformal}}+\mathcal{F}_{\text{conformal}},. $$

- • Conformal part: $\mathcal{F}_{\text{conformal}}\sim\sum_{h_{m}}c_{\Delta,m}F_{\Delta,m}(1,2,3,4)$ - has the form of the conformal partial wave expansion in a $1$ D CFT.

- • Non-conformal part:

$$ \mathcal{F}_{\text{non-conformal}}\sim\beta J\sum_{n}\text{Res}_{h=2}\left[\frac{k(h,n)}{1-k(h,n)}\rho(h)\right]\psi_{2,n}^{*}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})\psi_{2,n}(\tau_{3},\tau_{4})\,. $$

(15) Here $k(h,n)$ is the ladder kernel eigenvalue, and $\psi_{2,n}$ are the $h=2$ eigenfunctions of the symmetric ladder kernel (10).

The non-conformal contributions to two-point functions (12),(13) are constructed analogously.

## 3 Cutting rules for planar amplitudes

### 3.1 Derivation

Let us consider a vertex $V$ of order $4$ or higher. Then we can always cut it in such a way that the cut crosses two solid lines and nothing else, see Fig.3. Suppose that we cut through propagators $G(\tau_{a},\tau_{b})$ and $G(\tau_{c},\tau_{d})$ , which connect two vertices $U_{1}({\bf\tau}_{1},\tau_{a},\tau_{d})$ and $U_{2}({\bf\tau}_{2},\tau_{b},\tau_{c})$ . Here we denote all the time variables which are untouched by cut propagators by bold letters. In this case, we can write the vertex as

$$ V=U_{1}({\bf\tau}_{1},\tau_{a},\tau_{d})G(\tau_{a},\tau_{b})G(\tau_{c},\tau_{d})U_{2}({\bf\tau}_{2},\tau_{b},\tau_{c})\,. $$

Now we can rewrite the product of propagators through the ladder kernel using the definition (10):

$$ G(\tau_{a},\tau_{b})G(\tau_{c},\tau_{d})=\frac{\tilde{K}(\tau_{a},\tau_{d};\tau_{b},\tau_{c})}{(q-1)J^{2}|G(\tau_{a},\tau_{d})||G(\tau_{b},\tau_{c})|}\,. $$

We can diagonalize the ladder kernel using the system of its (normalized) eigenfunctions $\psi_{h,n}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})$ :

$$ \tilde{K}(\tau_{a},\tau_{d};\tau_{b},\tau_{c})=\sum_{h,n}k(h,n)\psi_{h,n}^{*}(\tau_{a},\tau_{d})\psi_{h,n}(\tau_{b},\tau_{c})\,. $$

Substituting (19) into (18) and then into (17), we obtain

$$ V=\sum_{h,n}k(h,n)U_{1}({\bf\tau}_{1},\tau_{a},\tau_{d})\frac{\psi_{h,n}^{*}(\tau_{a},\tau_{d})}{|G(\tau_{a},\tau_{d})|}\frac{\psi_{h,n}(\tau_{b},\tau_{c})}{|G(\tau_{b},\tau_{c})|}U_{2}({\bf\tau}_{2},\tau_{b},\tau_{c})\,. $$

Thus, we the vertex $V$ has a form of sum over products of smaller vertices $U_{1}$ and $U_{2}$ , which are connected by the "partial waves" $\psi_{h}$ .

In principle, one can cut the diagrams along the pairs of solid lines as much as needed, as long as each solid line is cut no more than once. ### 3.3 The six-point function example

where on r.h.s. the fields are averaged with respect to the quadratic action (9). We assume that one of the external lines is determined by the nonconformal contribution to the propagator, whereas the other two are conformal, as shown on the left side of the Fig.5. The Wick contractions give a factor $3!=6$ . The vertex gives the factor of $NJ^{6}/6$ , whereas the external propagators give a factor $\frac{2}{NJ^{2}}$ each. The expression for the planar diagram reads

$$ \displaystyle S_{2}=\frac{8}{N^{2}}\int dt_{1}dt_{2}dt_{3}dt_{4}dt_{5}dt_{6}\left(\frac{1}{\tilde{K}-1}\right)(\tau_{1},\tau_{2};t_{1},t_{2})|G(t_{12})|^{\frac{q-2}{2}}\times \displaystyle\left(\frac{1}{\tilde{K}-1}\right)(\tau_{3},\tau_{4};t_{3},t_{4})|G(t_{34})|^{\frac{q-2}{2}}\left(\frac{1}{\tilde{K}-1}\right)(\tau_{5},\tau_{6};t_{5},t_{6})|G(t_{56})|^{\frac{q-2}{2}}G(t_{23})G(t_{45})G(t_{61})\,. $$

Our approach is to cut the vertex in such a way that the We cut the diagram through the propagators $G(t_{23})$ and $G(t_{61})$ , as shown on Fig.5. Using (20), we write the correlator as

$$ \langle g(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})g(\tau_{3},\tau_{4})g(\tau_{5},\tau_{6})\rangle_{\text{planar}}\equiv S_{2}=3!\frac{NJ^{6}}{2\cdot 3}\sum_{h,n}k(h,n)U^{(1)}_{h,n}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})U^{(2)}_{h,n}(\tau_{3},\tau_{4};\tau_{5},\tau_{6})\,, $$

and we can evaluate $U$ -s separately. So,

$$ \displaystyle U^{(1)}_{h,n}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})=\int dt_{1}dt_{2}\langle g(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})\sigma(t_{1},t_{2})\rangle\frac{|G(t_{12})|}{|G(t_{12})|}\psi_{h,n}^{*}(t_{1},t_{2})\  $$

$$ =\frac{2}{NJ^{2}}\int dt_{1}dt_{2}\left(\frac{1}{\tilde{K}-1}\right)_{\text{non-conformal}}\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!(\tau_{1},\tau_{2};t_{1},t_{2})\psi_{h,n}^{*}(t_{1},t_{2})=\frac{2}{NJ^{2}}\frac{1}{k(2,n)-1}\psi_{2,n}^{*}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})\,. $$

This calculation shows that cutting away an external line of the planar diagram turns that external line simply expands the propagator in terms of the ladder eigenfunctions, and in particular, the non-conformal piece leaves just the $h=2$ eigenfunction. This reduces the number of integrations by $2$ . What is left to compute is the piece

$$ U^{(2)}_{2,n}=\int dt_{3}dt_{4}dt_{5}dt_{6}\frac{|G(t_{34})||G(t_{56})|}{|G(t_{36})|}G(t_{45})\psi_{2,n}(t_{3}.t_{6})\langle g(\tau_{3},\tau_{4})\sigma(t_{3},t_{4})\rangle\langle g(\tau_{5},\tau_{6})\sigma(t_{5},t_{6})\rangle\,. $$

The external lines of this piece are conformal, so one can take the OPE limit in them, analogously to the calculation of the fully conformal six-point function in [7]. In that case the $U^{(2)}$ reduces to a $3$ -loop integral, which is much simpler to evaluate. This method of cutting off the external non-conformal lines can be applied to reduce the integral in any hugher-point planar 1PI correlation function.

## Abstract

We study correlation functions of scalar operators on the boundary of the $AdS_{3}$ space deformed by moving massive particles in the context of the AdS/CFT duality. To calculate two-point correlation functions we use the geodesic approximation and the renormalized image method. We compare results of the renormalized image method with direct calculations using tracing of winding geodesics around the cone singularities, and show on examples that they are equivalent. We demonstrate that in the geodesic approximation the correlators exhibit a zone structure. This structure substantially depends on the mass and velocity of the particle.

#### Keywords

## 1 Introduction

The AdS/CFT, or more generally the gauge/gravity duality [1, 2, 3] is a powerful tool in the study of quantum systems in the strong coupling limit. Due to its flexibility there is a wide range of applications in heavy-ion collision [4, 5, 6], condensed matter theory [7, 8, 9], thermalization of strongly coupling theories [10, 11, 12, 13, 14], entanglement entropy [15, 16, 17] and quantum quenches [18, 19].

Two dimensional conformal field theory is the holographic dual of $AdS_{3}$ gravity. Three dimensional gravity is topological and there are no propagating gravitons in this theory. Deformations of the three-dimensional gravity by point particles are only global [20, 21]. This means, that locally the deformed space is still the $AdS_{3}$ , but globally there are wedges to cut out and glue their faces. In another words, point particles induce conical singularities. Scattering of point particles in the space with conical singularities was studied in [22]. Classical and quantum scalar field theories on a cone have been considered in several papers starting from [23] and scalar fields in the flat space with defects have been studied in [24]. The cosmic strings in the flat $M_{4}$ and $AdS_{4}$ provide four-dimensional generalization [25, 26, 27], while the cosmic membranes provide higher dimensional generalization of conical defect in the context of the TeV-gravity [28].

In is natural to ask a question about holographic dual to $AdS_{3}$ with point particles [29]. Correlators in the theory dual to $AdS_{3}$ with a static particle have been considered within the geodesic approximation [29, 30] and appearance of new excitations in the boundary theory has been noticed. Then, the AdS/CFT correspondence for the multi-boundary $AdS_{3}$ orbifold has been studied [31]. A new quantity, called entwinement, in the dual CFT has been introduced in [32], and it has been shown that it is related with the conical defect geometry. Correlators in the theory dual to the Gott time machine in the $AdS_{3}$ have been investigated [33]. A holographic dual model for defect conformal field theories has been considered in [34].

In this paper we continue to study boundary theories dual to $AdS_{3}$ deformed by massive moving point particles. To describe these deformations it is convenient to consider $AdS_{3}$ as an $SL(2,R)$ group manifold [35]. $AdS_{3}$ with a particle is a space that remains after cutting out a special subset, called wedge, from $AdS_{3}$ spacetime, and then identifying the boundaries of this wedge in a special way [21, 36]. The geodesics in this spacetime locally are the same as in the nondeformed $AdS_{3}$ and this drastically simplifies the problem of constructing the boundary correlators in the geodesic approximation. In the geodesic approximation one has to find all geodesics connecting two given points on the boundary. For one static particle one can find all geodesics connecting two spacelike separated points explicitly in the Deser-Jackiw coordinates [32]. But the generalization of these coordinates to multi-particle cases is not explicit [37] which makes the problem of analytical description of all geodesics rather complicated.

We study this problem using the cutting and gluing method that has been used previously in [29, 30, 32, 33]. As in [33], in this paper we have to use numerical simulations to take into account all geodesics connecting two given points on the boundary in the present of moving defects.

The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we remind the group structure of the $AdS_{3}$ and set the notations. In Section 3, the renormalized image method is described. The relation of winding geodesics and imaged geodesics is clarified on several examples. In Section 4, the zone structure of correlators on the boundary of the $AdS_{3}$ deformed by moving particle is presented and discussed.

### 2.2 Point particles in $AdS_{3}$

It is known, that the gravity in spacetime dimension 3 is almost trivial, in the sense of absence of propagating degrees of freedom. In works [20, 21] it was shown, that point particle does not change the metric locally, producing conical defect singularity. In this section we remind the structure of the $AdS_{3}$ deformed by point particles.

#### 2.2.1 Static particle in $AdS_{3}$

Let us recall the Deser-Jackiw solution [20]. Consider the Einstein equation in the 3-dimensional spacetime with the cosmological constant which equals to $-1$ :

$$ G^{\mu\nu}-g^{\mu\nu}=8\pi GT^{\mu\nu}. $$

The ansatz for the metric $ds_{DJ}^{2}$ supported by the time independent point-like source is:

$$ \displaystyle ds_{DJ}^{2} \displaystyle= \displaystyle-N^{2}(R)dt^{2}+\Phi(R)(dR^{2}+R^{2}d\tilde{\phi}^{2}), \displaystyle T^{00} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{m}{\sqrt{-g}}N(R)\delta(R), $$

where functions $\Phi(R)$ and $N(R)$ are:

$$ \displaystyle\Phi(R)=\frac{4A^{2}}{\Lambda R^{2}(\left(R/R_{0})^{A}+(R/R_{0})^{-A}\right)^{2}},\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,N(R)=\frac{(\left(R/R_{0})^{A}-(R/R_{0})^{-A}\right)}{(\left(R/R_{0})^{A}+(R/R_{0})^{-A}\right)} $$

Parameter $A$ connects with the mass of the particle as $A=1-4Gm$ . After the change of variables:

$$ \displaystyle\sinh\chi=\frac{1}{2}\left(\left(\frac{R}{R_{0}}\right)^{A}+\left(\frac{R}{R_{0}}\right)^{-A}\right),\,\,\,\,\,\,\phi=A\tilde{\phi}, $$

we get the $AdS_{3}$ metric in the barrel coordinates with a different angular coordinate range of values,

$$ \displaystyle ds^{2}=-\cosh^{2}\chi dt^{2}+d\chi^{2}+\sinh^{2}\chi d\phi^{2},\,\,\,\,\,\,\phi\in\left(0,2\pi A\right). $$

Let us now consider the static particle case from the group language. Resting in the center of the $AdS_{3}$ static particle cuts out the wedge that can be described by two faces that are some constant angle surfaces (see Fig.1). These two faces are identified in the constant $t$ sections. In matrix notation the first face of the wedge is:

$$ {\bf x}_{1-st\,face}=\cosh\chi\,{\bf\Omega}(t)+\sinh\chi\,{\bf\Gamma}(-\alpha/2). $$

The face is parameterized by two values: $\alpha$ and $t$ , $\alpha$ is proportional to the mass of the particle and $t$ is time coordinate. The second face of the wedge can be obtained by rotation of the first face by the angle $\alpha$ . Writing out rotation:

$$ {\bf x}_{rot}=u_{rot}^{-1}\,{\bf x}\,u_{rot},\,\,\,\,\,\,u_{rot}={\bf\Omega}(-\alpha/2), $$

we get the second face:

$$ {\bf x}_{2-nd\,face}={\bf\Omega}(\alpha/2)\,\cdot\,{\bf x}_{1-st\,face}\,\cdot\,{\bf\Omega}(-\alpha/2), $$

where ${\bf\Omega}(\alpha/2)$ is given by (2.5).

#### 2.2.2 Moving massive particle in the $AdS_{3}$

To consider a massive moving particle and get it’s group language description one can consider a static particle and boost it. The massive particle moves along the periodic worldline oscillating in the bulk of the $AdS_{3}$ . The constant angle faces of the wedge to be identified become some surfaces that one can get by boosting the wedge of the static particle. These faces are glued as in the static case along the constant time slices and symmetrically with respect to the boost direction, but now they exhibit some nontrivial isometry due to nontrivial holonomy induced by the moving particle.

To obtain the faces of the wedge of moving massive particle we make the boost, that in the matrix notation has the form:

$$ \displaystyle{\mathbb{u}}=\cosh(\xi/2)\,{\bf 1}-\sinh(\xi/2)\,\gamma_{2}=\cosh(\xi/2)\,{\bf\Omega}(0)-\sinh(\xi/2)\,{\bf\Gamma}(\pi/2), $$

i.e. we apply (2.9) to the faces of the wedge (2.7) and (2.8) and get:

$$ \displaystyle{\bf x}_{1\,-\,mov\,-\,face}={\mathbb{u}}^{-1}{\bf x}_{1\,-\,face}{\mathbb{u}},\,\,\,\,{\bf x}_{2\,-\,mov\,-\,face}={\mathbb{u}}^{-1}{\bf x}_{2\,-\,face}{\mathbb{u}}. $$

From (2.8) we find the isometry map identifying these two wedges:

$$ \displaystyle{\bf x}_{2-nd\,mov\,\,face} \displaystyle= \displaystyle{\bf\Omega}_{{\mathbb{u}}}(\alpha/2,\xi/2)\,\cdot\,{\bf x}_{1-st\,mov\,\,face}\,\cdot\,{\bf\Omega}_{{\mathbb{u}}}(-\alpha/2,\xi/2), $$

where

$$ {\bf\Omega}_{{\mathbb{u}}}(-\alpha/2,\xi/2)\equiv{\bf\Omega}_{{\mathbb{u}}}={\mathbb{u}}^{-1}(\xi/2){\bf\Omega}\left(-\alpha/{2}\right){\mathbb{u}}(\xi/2). $$

Finally the isometry induced by the presence of the moving massive particle in $\text{AdS}_{3}$ is:

$$ {\bf x}^{*}={\bf\Omega}_{{\mathbb{u}}}^{-1}{\bf x}{\bf\Omega}_{{\mathbb{u}}}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}x_{3}^{*}+x_{2}^{*}&x_{0}^{*}+x_{1}^{*}\\
x_{1}^{*}-x_{0}^{*}&x_{3}^{*}-x_{2}^{*}\\
\end{array}\right), $$

where x is the $AdS_{3}$ point defined as (2.3).

Rewriting (2.3) in an explicit form using barrel coordinates:

$$ {\bf x}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}\cos t\cosh\chi+\sin\phi\sinh\chi&\cosh\chi\sin t+\cos\phi\sinh\chi\\
-\cosh\chi\sin t+\cos\phi\sinh\chi&\cos t\cosh\chi-\sin\phi\sinh\chi\\
\end{array}\right), $$

and (2.12) has the form:

$$ {\bf x}^{*}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}\cos t^{*}\cosh\chi^{*}+\sin\phi^{*}\sinh\chi^{*}&\cosh\chi^{*}\sin t^{*}+\cos\phi^{*}\sinh\chi^{*}\\
-\cosh\chi^{*}\sin t^{*}+\cos\phi^{*}\sinh\chi^{*}&\cos t^{*}\cosh\chi^{*}-\sin\phi^{*}\sinh\chi^{*}\\
\end{array}\right). $$

After some algebra we get an explicit coordinate expression for isometry as:

$$ \displaystyle\tan t^{*} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\mathcal{B}_{\xi}(\alpha)\sec t\tanh\chi\cos\phi+\tan t\left(1+2\sinh^{2}\xi\sin^{2}\frac{\alpha}{2}\right), \displaystyle\tan\phi^{*} \displaystyle= \displaystyle-2\mathcal{\xi(\alpha)}^{-1}\tan\phi, $$

$$ \displaystyle\cosh\chi^{*} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\cosh\chi[\left(\mathcal{B}_{\xi}(\alpha)\tanh\chi\cos\phi+\sin t(1+2\sinh^{2}\xi\sin^{2}\frac{\alpha}{2})\right)^{2}+\cos^{2}t]^{\frac{1}{2}}, $$

where

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{B}_{\xi}(\alpha) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sinh\xi\left(\sin\alpha\tan\phi-2\cosh\xi\sin^{2}\frac{\alpha}{2}\right), \displaystyle\mathcal{\xi(\alpha)} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\cosh\xi(2\sin\alpha\tan\phi-\cos\alpha+\cos\phi) \displaystyle+ \displaystyle\sec\phi\cos(\alpha+\phi)+\cos\alpha\cosh 2\xi-2\sinh^{2}\xi. $$

From (2.13) taking the limit $\chi\rightarrow\infty$ we get the expression for isometry near the boundary of the $AdS_{3}$ :

$$ \displaystyle\tan t_{b}^{*} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\mathcal{B}_{\xi}(\alpha)\sec t_{b}\cos\phi_{b}+\tan t_{b}\left(1+2\sinh^{2}\xi\sin^{2}\frac{\alpha}{2}\right), \displaystyle\tan\phi_{b}^{*} \displaystyle= \displaystyle-{2\mathcal{\xi(\alpha)}^{-1}\tan\phi_{b}}. $$

The expression for the radial coordinate $\chi$ after the isometry near the boundary is:

$$ \displaystyle\text{e}^{\chi_{nb}^{*}} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\text{e}^{\chi_{nb}}\sqrt{\mathcal{A}}\,, $$

where

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{A} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\left(\mathcal{B}_{\xi}(\alpha)\cos\phi_{b}+\sin t_{b}(1+2\sinh^{2}\xi\sin^{2}\frac{\alpha}{2})\right)^{2}+\cos^{2}t_{b}. $$

Now we derive equations defining the wedge faces. As it has been mentioned above, to fix the wedges we must find points that are constant in time and symmetrical in angle under the isometry, i.e. they are fixed by conditions $t^{*}=t$ and $\phi^{*}=-\phi$ . So, solving equation $\tan t=\tan t^{*}$ we get the expression for the wedge face:

$$ \displaystyle\tanh\chi \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{2\sin t\sinh\xi\sin^{2}\frac{\alpha}{2}}{2\cosh\xi\sin^{2}\frac{\alpha}{2}\cos\phi\pm\sin\alpha\sin\phi}. $$

It is useful to change the variable as $r=\tanh(\chi/2)$ and get $r$ as function of $\phi$ and $t$ for two wedges:

$$ \displaystyle r(\phi,t) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\tanh\left(\frac{1}{2}\text{arctanh}\frac{2\sin t\sinh\xi\sin^{2}\frac{\alpha}{2}}{2\cosh\xi\sin^{2}\frac{\alpha}{2}\cos\phi\pm\sin\alpha\sin\phi}\right). $$

The intersection of two surfaces determined by (2.18) gives a fixed point of the isometry (or equally the massive particle worldline):

$$ \displaystyle r(t) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{1-\sqrt{1-\tanh^{2}\xi\sin^{2}t}}{\tanh\xi\sin t}. $$

The massive particle moves from the left to right and vice versa periodically (with period $T=2\pi$ ). Note that if $\xi\rightarrow\infty$ we will obtain the case of massless moving particle $r=\tan(t/2)$ that coincides with formulas for the massless particle in paper [35]. For constant time $t$ slices the wedge faces are some curves intersecting at the particle position. The angle $\phi_{w}$ between these two curves at the intersection point can be expressed as:

$$ \varphi=\arctan\left(\frac{4\sin^{2}\frac{\alpha}{2}\sin\alpha\cosh\xi\sqrt{1-\sin^{2}t\tanh^{2}\xi}}{\sin^{2}\alpha-4\sin^{4}\frac{\alpha}{2}\left(1+2\sinh^{2}\xi\sin^{2}\frac{\alpha}{2}\right)}\right). $$

From this formula we can see, that the angle $\phi_{w}$ is maximal at $t=\pm\frac{\pi}{2}$ if $\alpha>\pi$ and at $t=0$ if $\alpha<\pi$ (see Fig.2).

### 2.3 Correlation functions on the boundary and geodesics in the $AdS_{3}$ .

In the AdS/CFT correspondence, to calculate the two-point correlation function of a scalar operator $\Phi_{\Delta}$ with large conformal weight $\Delta$ on the $AdS_{3}$ boundary, one can use the geodesic approximation [29]. In this approximation one defines the correlator:

$$ G_{\Delta}(\phi_{a},t_{a};\phi_{b},t_{b})=e^{-\Delta{\cal L}_{ren}(\phi_{a},t_{a};\phi_{b},t_{b})}. $$

Here $a$ and $b$ are two points on the boundary of the $AdS_{3}$ with coordinates $(\phi_{a},t_{a})$ and $(\phi_{b},t_{b})$ . For the spacelike separated points $a$ and $b$ , ${\cal L}_{ren}(\phi_{a},t_{a};\phi_{b},t_{b})$ is the renormalized length of the geodesic connecting these points [29, 30]. If $a$ and $b$ are timelike separated points, there is no geodesic between them. In the paper we restrict ourselves to the geodesics between spacelike-separated points. The contribution of timelike separated points from the geodesic prescription is considered in the next paper.

#### 2.3.1 Spacelike separated points

Now we remind how the geodesic approximation works in the $AdS_{3}$ global coordinates. We consider two spacelike separated boundary points $(\phi_{a},t_{a})$ and $(\phi_{b},t_{b})$ . We assume for definiteness $\phi_{b}>\phi_{a}$ . The geodesic curve in the bulk $(\phi,t,r)=(\phi(\lambda),t(\lambda),r(\lambda))$ , connecting these points is given by :

$$ \displaystyle\phi_{ab}(\lambda) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\arctan\left(\tan\frac{D_{s}[\phi_{a},\phi_{b}]}{2}\cdot\tanh\lambda\right)+\Sigma_{s}[\phi_{a},\phi_{b}], \displaystyle t_{ab}(\lambda) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\arctan\left(\tan\frac{D[t_{a},t_{b}]}{2}\cdot\tanh\lambda\right)+\Sigma[t_{a},t_{b}] $$

and

$$ \displaystyle r(\lambda) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{\sqrt{\cos(2D[t_{a},t_{b}]+\cosh(2\lambda)}-\sqrt{\cos(2D[t_{a},t_{b}]-\cos(2D_{s}[\phi_{a},\phi_{b}]))}}{\sqrt{\cos(2D_{s}[\phi_{a},\phi_{b}])+\cosh(2\lambda)}}. $$

Here the parametrization is taken so that the parameter value $\lambda=-\infty$ corresponds to the point $(\phi_{a},t_{a})$ on the boundary and $\lambda=+\infty$ corresponds to the point $(\phi_{b},t_{b})$ . $D_{s}[\phi_{a},\phi_{b}]$ , $D[t_{a},t_{b}]$ , $\Sigma_{s}[\phi_{a},\phi_{b}]$ and $\Sigma[t_{a},t_{b}]$ are defined as

$$ \displaystyle\phi_{b}-\phi_{a}<\pi:\,\,\,\,\,\,D_{s}[\phi_{a},\phi_{b}] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\phi_{b}-\phi_{a}, \displaystyle\Sigma_{s}[\phi_{a},\phi_{b}] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{\phi_{b}+\phi_{a}}{2}; \displaystyle\phi_{b}-\phi_{a}>\pi:\,\,\,\,\,\,D_{s}[\phi_{a},\phi_{b}] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\phi_{b}-\phi_{a}-2\pi, \displaystyle\Sigma_{s}[\phi_{a},\phi_{b}] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{\phi_{b}+\phi_{a}}{2}+\pi; \displaystyle D[t_{a},t_{b}] \displaystyle= \displaystyle t_{b}-t_{a}, \displaystyle\Sigma[t_{a},t_{b}] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{t_{b}+t_{a}}{2}. $$

Note, that in [33] another parametrization for this geodesic has been used.

It is easy to calculate the geodesic length ${\cal L}_{AdS}$ between two points on the curve (2.20)-(2.21) using

$$ \displaystyle\cosh{\cal L}_{AdS} \displaystyle= \displaystyle-\frac{1}{2}\left[\det({\bf x}_{a}-{\bf x}_{b})-2\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle-(x_{(a)},x_{(b)})=x_{0,a}x_{0,b}+x_{3,a}x_{3,b}-x_{1,a}x_{1,b}-x_{2,a}x_{2,b}, $$

where $x_{i,a}$ and $x_{i,b}$ , $i=0,1,2,3$ are embedding coordinates (2.2) of the endpoints. Writing down (2.23) explicitly in coordinates $(\phi,t,\chi)$ we express the geodesic length between points $a=(\phi_{a},t_{a},\chi_{a})$ and $b=(\phi_{b},t_{b},\chi_{b})$ as:

$$ \displaystyle- \displaystyle\cosh{\cal L}(a;b)= \displaystyle= \displaystyle-\cosh\chi_{a}\,\sin t_{a}\cosh\chi_{b}\,\sin t_{b}-\cosh\chi_{a}\,\cos t_{a}\cosh\chi_{b}\,\cos t_{b} \displaystyle+ \displaystyle\sinh\chi_{a}\,\cos\phi_{a}\sinh\chi_{b}\,\cos\phi_{b}+\sinh\chi_{a}\sin\phi_{a}\sinh\chi_{b}\sin\phi_{b}. $$

When points $a$ and $b$ go to the boundary (i.e. $\chi_{a,b}\to\infty$ ) one gets:

$$ \displaystyle{\cal L}_{reg}(a;b) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\ln\left[\left(\cos(t_{a}-t_{b})-\cos(\phi_{a}-\phi_{b})\right)\frac{e^{\chi_{a}+\chi_{b}}}{2}\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\ln\left[2(\cos(t_{a}-t_{b})-\cos(\phi_{a}-\phi_{b}))\right]+\delta_{a}+\delta_{b}, $$

where $\delta_{a}=\chi_{a}-\ln 2$ and $\delta_{b}=\chi_{b}-\ln 2$ .

Removing the divergent parts $\delta_{a}$ , $\delta_{b}$ in (2.25) we get the renormalized geodesic length for the spacelike geodesic connecting two points on the boundary:

$$ {\cal L}_{ren}(t_{a},\phi_{a};t_{b},\phi_{b})=\ln[2\left(\cos(t_{a}-t_{b})-\cos(\phi_{a}-\phi_{b})\right)], $$

From this formula and (2.19) the two-point function on the $AdS_{3}$ boundary is:

$$ G_{\Delta,AdS}\left(\phi_{a},t_{a},\phi_{b},t_{b}\right)=\left(\frac{1}{2(\cos(t_{a}-t_{b})-\cos(\phi_{a}-\phi_{b}))}\right)^{\Delta}. $$

#### 2.3.2 Timelike separated points

Mentioned above, there are no continous geodesics in the $AdS_{3}$ connecting two timelike separated points on the boundary. So, to use the geodesic approximation in calculation of two-point functions for timelike separated points, we use the prescription proposed in [30, 33]. This prescription is related with the prescription that has been early proposed in [11] in the Poincare patch. According to this prescription to calculate the correlator for timelike separated points one has to relate these points by a quasigeodesic, that consists of two pieces of the spacelike geodesics with a discontinuity at the Poincare horizon. The explicit formulae are

$$ \displaystyle\phi_{ab}(\lambda) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\arctan\left(\tan\frac{D[\phi_{a},\phi_{b}]}{2}\cdot\coth\lambda\right)+\Sigma[\phi_{a},\phi_{b}], \displaystyle t_{ab}(\lambda) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\arctan\left(\tan\frac{D[t_{a},t_{b}]}{2}\cdot\coth\lambda\right)+\Sigma[t_{a},t_{b}], $$

and

$$ \displaystyle r(\lambda)=\frac{\sqrt{\cos(2D[t_{a},t_{b}])+\cosh(2\lambda)}-\sqrt{\cos(2D[t_{a},t_{b}])-\cos(2D[\phi_{a},\phi_{b}]))}}{\sqrt{\cos(2D[\phi_{a},\phi_{b}]))+\cosh(2\lambda)}}, $$

where $D[t_{a},t_{b}]$ and $\Sigma[t_{a},t_{b}]$ are defined as (2.22)

In Fig.4 we plot the quasigeodesic corresponding to the boundary points $a$ and $b$ with coordinates $(\phi_{a},t_{a})$ and $(\phi_{b},t_{b})$ , respectively.

For simplicity we consider the case of symmetric points. In this case the boundary points are taken to be $(\delta\phi,\delta t)$ , $(-\delta\phi,-\delta t)$ , where

$$ \delta\phi=\frac{\phi_{a}-\phi_{b}}{2},\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\delta t=\frac{t_{a}-t_{b}}{2}. $$

The part of the quasigeodesic that starts at the point $a$ at $\lambda=-\infty$ reaches the Poincare horizon at the point with coordinates $(\phi_{h_{1}},t_{h_{1}},\chi_{h_{1}})$ . These coordinates correspond to the values of the right hand side of formulae (2.28)-(2.30) at $\lambda\to-0$ :

$$ \displaystyle t_{h_{1}}=-\frac{\pi}{2},\,\,\,\,\,\phi_{h_{1}}=-\frac{\pi}{2},\,\,\,\,\,\chi_{h_{1}}={\mbox{arcsinh}}\frac{|\sin\delta\phi|}{\sqrt{\sin^{2}\delta t-\sin^{2}\delta\phi}}. $$

The part of the quasigeodesic that reaches the point $b$ at $\lambda=+\infty$ starts from the Poincare horizon at the point with coordinates $(\phi_{h_{2}},t_{h_{2}},\chi_{h_{2}})$ , that correspond to the values of the right hand side of formulae (2.28)-(2.30) at $\lambda\to+0$ :

$$ \displaystyle t_{h_{2}}=\frac{\pi}{2},\,\,\,\,\phi_{h_{2}}=\frac{\pi}{2},\,\,\,\,\chi_{h_{2}}={\mbox{arcsinh}}\frac{|\sin\delta\phi|}{\sqrt{\sin^{2}\delta t-\sin^{2}\delta\phi}}. $$

Taking $b=h_{1}$ and $a=a_{r}$ in formula (2.24) we get the geodesic length between $a_{r}$ , the point near the boundary (i.e. $\chi$ is large) with coordinates $(-\delta\phi,-\delta t,\chi)$ and the point $h_{1}$ with coordinates $(\phi_{h_{1}},t_{h_{1}},\chi_{h_{1}})$ :

$$ \displaystyle{\cal L}(a_{r};h_{1})=\ln\left(2\sqrt{\sin^{2}\delta t-\sin^{2}\delta\phi\,}\right)\,+\delta_{a_{r}}+...,\,\,\,\,\,\,\delta_{a_{r}}=\chi_{a_{r}}-\ln 2, $$

where dots mean subleading terms when $\chi\to\infty$ . Subtracting the linear on $\chi$ term we get the renormalized geodesic length between the point $a$ on the boundary and point $h_{1}$ :

$$ {\cal L}_{ren}(a;h_{1})=\ln\left(2\sqrt{\sin^{2}\delta t-\sin^{2}\delta\phi\,}\right). $$

In a similar way taking $b=h_{2}$ and $a=b_{r}$ in formula (2.24) and subtracting the divergent term $\delta_{b_{r}}=\chi_{b_{r}}-\ln 2$ we get the renormalized geodesic length between the point $b$ on the boundary and the point $h_{2}$ on the Poincare horizon:

$$ {\cal L}_{ren}(b;h_{2})=\ln\left(2\sqrt{\sin^{2}\delta t-\sin^{2}\delta\phi\,}\right). $$

Summing (2.33) and (2.34) we get

$$ \displaystyle{\cal L}_{quasi,ren}(t_{a},\phi_{a};t_{b},\phi_{b})={\cal L}_{ren}(a;h_{1})+{\cal L}_{ren}(b;h_{2}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle 2\ln(2\sqrt{\sin^{2}\delta t-\sin^{2}\delta\phi})=\ln(2(-\cos(t_{a}-t_{b})+\cos(\phi_{a}-\phi_{b}))), $$

Combining (2.35) with the (2.19) we get the answer for the two-point correlation function for timelike separated points

$$ G_{\Delta,AdS}\left(\phi_{a},t_{a},\phi_{b},t_{b}\right)=\left(\frac{1}{2(-\cos(t_{a}-t_{b})+\cos(\phi_{a}-\phi_{b}))}\right)^{\Delta}. $$

Comparing (2.27) and (2.36) we can write

$$ G_{\Delta,AdS}\left(\phi_{a},t_{a},\phi_{b},t_{b}\right)=\left(\frac{1}{2|\cos(t_{a}-t_{b})-\cos(\phi_{a}-\phi_{b})|}\right)^{\Delta}. $$

#### 2.3.3 Reflection symmetry

As has been noted in [33] the correlator (2.37) possesses the reflection symmetry,

$$ G_{\Delta,AdS}(\phi_{a},t_{a};\phi_{b},t_{b})=G_{\Delta,AdS}(\phi_{a},t_{a};\phi_{b}+\pi,t_{b}+\pi), $$

i.e. this correlator is invariant under a shift on $\pi$ of both arguments $t$ and $\phi$ simultaneously. The transformation $(t,\phi)\to(t+\pi,\phi+\pi)$ is the reflection transformation. Under this transformation the timelike interval $ab$ transforms to the spacelike one $ab^{\prime\prime}$ and vice versa (see Fig.5).

#### 2.3.4 Remarks about the Wightman, causal and retarded correlators

Let us note the relation of the function (2.37) defined via the geodesics approximation with the causal, retarded and Wightman correlators. The Wightman correlators are obtained [38, 39, 40] by the $i\epsilon$ prescription from the CFT correlators on the Euclidean cylinder

$$ G_{E}(\phi_{a},\tau_{a};,\phi_{b},\tau_{b})=\left(\frac{1}{2(\cosh(\tau_{a}-\tau_{b})-\cos(\phi_{a}-\phi_{b}))}\right)^{\Delta}. $$

and can be written as

$$ \displaystyle G_{W}(\phi_{a},t_{a};\phi_{b},t_{b}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\langle O(\phi_{a},t_{a})O(\phi_{b},t_{b})\rangle \displaystyle= \displaystyle\left(\frac{1}{2(\cos(t_{a}-t_{b}-i\epsilon)-\cos(\phi_{a}-\phi_{b}))}\right)^{\Delta} $$

In the sense of distributions [41] we can present (2.39) as

$$ \displaystyle G_{W}(\phi_{a},t_{a};\phi_{b},t_{b})=G_{\Delta,AdS}(\phi_{a},t_{a};\phi_{b},t_{b}) \displaystyle\cdot \displaystyle\left\{\Psi_{W}(t_{a};t_{b})\,\theta(-\cos(t_{a}-t_{b})+\cos(\phi_{a}-\phi_{b})]+\theta(\cos(t_{a}-t_{b})-\cos(\phi_{a}-\phi_{b}))\right\} $$

where $G_{\Delta,AdS}$ is defined as (2.37) and $\Psi_{W}$ function is:

$$ \displaystyle\Psi_{W}(t_{a};t_{b}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle e^{-i\,\pi\,\Delta\,\,{\mbox{sign}}(\sin(t_{a}-t_{b}))}. $$

Using (2.39) one gets the representation for the causal correlator of the conformal fields on the cylinder:

$$ \displaystyle G_{c}(\phi_{a},t_{a};\phi_{b},t_{b}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\langle TO(\phi_{a},t_{a})O(\phi_{b},t_{b})\rangle_{c} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\left(\frac{1}{2(\cos(t_{a}-t_{b}-i\epsilon(t_{a}-t_{b}))-\cos(\phi_{a}-\phi_{b}))}\right)^{\Delta}, $$

that can be written as

$$ \displaystyle G_{c}(\phi_{a},t_{a};\phi_{b},t_{b})=G_{\Delta,AdS}(\phi_{a},t_{a};\phi_{b},t_{b}) \displaystyle\cdot \displaystyle\left\{\Psi_{c}(t_{a};t_{b})\,\theta(-\cos(t_{a}-t_{b})+\cos(\phi_{a}-\phi_{b}))+\theta(\cos(t_{a}-t_{b})-\cos(\phi_{a}-\phi_{b}))\right\}, $$

where

$$ \displaystyle\Psi_{c}(t_{a};t_{b}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle e^{-i\,\pi\,\Delta\,\,{\mbox{sign}}(\sin(t_{a}-t_{b}))}\,\theta(t_{a}-t_{b})+e^{i\pi\,\Delta\,{\mbox{sign}}(\sin(t_{a}-t_{b}))}\,\theta(-t_{a}+t_{b}). $$

The retarded correlator can be represented as

$$ \displaystyle G_{ret}(\phi_{a},t_{a};\phi_{b},t_{b}) \displaystyle\equiv \displaystyle\theta(t_{a}-t_{b})\langle[O(\phi_{a},t_{a}),O(\phi_{b},t_{b})]\rangle, $$

and then we have

$$ \displaystyle G {}_{ret}(\phi_{a},t_{a};\phi_{b},t_{b})= \displaystyle= \displaystyle G_{\Delta,AdS}(\phi_{a},t_{a};\phi_{b},t_{b})\Psi_{ret}(t_{a};t_{b})\cdot\,\theta(t_{a}-t_{b})\theta(-\cos(t_{a}-t_{b})+\cos(\phi_{a}-\phi_{b})), $$

where

$$ \displaystyle\Psi_{ret}(t_{a};t_{b})=-2i\sin(\pi\Delta\,{\mbox{sign}}(\sin(t_{a}-t_{b}))). $$

The above formula can be written in the universal way

$$ \displaystyle G_{A,\Delta}(\phi_{a},t_{a};\phi_{b},t_{b}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle G_{\Delta,AdS}(\phi_{a},t_{a};\phi_{b},t_{b})\cdot\Phi_{A,\Delta}(\phi_{a},t_{a};\phi_{b},t_{b}), $$

where the subscript $A$ means Wightman $(W)$ , causal $(c)$ or retarded $(r)$ and

$$ \displaystyle\Phi {}_{B,\Delta}(\phi_{a},t_{a};\phi_{b},t_{b})= \displaystyle= \displaystyle\Psi_{B,\Delta}(t_{a};t_{b})\cdot\,\theta(-\cos(t_{a}-t_{b})+\cos(\phi_{a}-\phi_{b}))+\theta(\cos(t_{a}-t_{b})-\cos(\phi_{a}-\phi_{b})) \displaystyle\Phi {}_{ret,\Delta}(\phi_{a},t_{a};\phi_{b},t_{b})= \displaystyle= \displaystyle\Psi_{ret,\Delta}(t_{a};t_{b})\cdot\,\theta(t_{a}-t_{b})\theta(-\cos(t_{a}-t_{b})+\cos(\phi_{a}-\phi_{b})), $$

and where subscript $B$ stands for Wightman $(W)$ or causal $(c)$ .

For an integer $\Delta$ the functions defined by (2.3.4) and (2.42) coincide and the factor $\Psi_{ret}$ is zero.

## 3 Image method and winding geodesics

### 3.1 Image method on the living space

When the $AdS_{3}$ is deformed by the point particle, formulae (2.39), (2.41) and (2.43) have to be modified. In particular,

$$ \displaystyle<TO(\phi_{a},t_{a})O(\phi_{b},t_{b})>_{l.s.}= \displaystyle= \displaystyle\left(\frac{1}{2(\cos(t_{a}-t_{b}+i(t_{a}-t_{b})\epsilon)-\cos(\phi_{a}-\phi_{b}))}\right)^{\Delta}\Theta_{0}(\phi_{a},t_{a};\phi_{b},t_{b}) \displaystyle+ \displaystyle\sum_{n\in Z}\left(\frac{1}{2(\cos(t^{*}_{a,n}-t_{b}+i(t^{*}_{a,n}-t_{b})\epsilon)-\cos(\phi^{*}_{a,n}-\phi_{b}))}\right)^{\Delta}\Theta_{n}(\phi^{*}_{a,n},t^{*}_{a,n};\phi_{b},t_{b})Z_{n}(\phi^{*}_{a,n},t^{*}_{a,n};\phi_{b},t_{b}) \displaystyle+ \displaystyle\sum_{n\in Z}\left(\frac{1}{2(\cos(t^{\#}_{a,n}-t_{b}+i(t^{\#}_{a,n}-t_{b})\epsilon)-\cos(\phi^{*}_{a,n}-\phi_{b}))}\right)^{\Delta}\bar{\Theta}_{n}(\phi^{\#}_{a,n},t^{\#}_{a,n};\phi_{b},t_{b})\bar{Z_{n}}(\phi^{\#}_{a,n},t^{\#}_{a,n};\phi_{b},t_{b}) $$

Here the subscript l.s. in the LHS of (3.46) means a living space of the boundary of the $AdS_{3}$ with static or moving defects and

$$ (\phi_{a},t_{a})^{*\,n}=(\phi^{*}_{a,n},t^{*}_{a,n}), $$

are coordinates of the image points obtained by n-times applications of the isometry *-transformation (2.12). The $\#$ -transformation is defined so that

$$ (\phi_{a}^{\#}\,t_{a}^{\#})^{*}=(\phi_{a},t_{a}), $$

and we also use notations

$$ (\phi_{a},t_{a})^{\#\,n}=(\phi^{\#}_{a,n},t^{\#}_{a,n}). $$

where $G_{\Delta,AdS}(\phi_{a},t_{a};\phi_{b},t_{b})$ is given by (2.37) and $\Phi_{c,\Delta}(\phi_{a},t_{a};\phi_{b},t_{b})$ by (2.44).

we get

$$ \displaystyle G_{l.s.}(\phi_{a},t_{a},\phi_{b},t_{b}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle G_{\Delta,AdS}(\phi_{a},t_{a};\phi_{b},t_{b})\,\Theta_{0}(\phi_{a},t_{a};\phi_{b},t_{b}) \displaystyle+ \displaystyle\sum_{n}\,G_{\Delta,ren,n}(\phi^{*}_{a,n},t^{*}_{a,n};\phi_{b},t_{b})\,\Theta_{n}(\phi^{*}_{a,n},t^{*}_{a,n};\phi_{b},t_{b}) \displaystyle+ \displaystyle\sum_{n}\,G_{\Delta,ren,n}(\phi^{\#}_{a,n},t^{\#}_{a,n};\phi_{b},t_{b})\,\bar{\Theta}_{n}(\phi^{\#}_{a,n},t^{\#}_{a,n};\phi_{b},t_{b}), $$

and in one keeps the isometry invariance in the renormalization prescription then the following properties take place:

$$ \displaystyle G_{\Delta,ren,n}(\phi^{*}_{a,n},t^{*}_{a,n};\phi_{b},t_{b}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle G_{\Delta,ren,n}(\phi^{*}_{a,n-1},t^{*}_{a,n-1};\phi^{\#}_{b,1},t^{\#}_{b,1})=G_{\Delta,ren,n}(\phi_{a},t_{a};\phi^{\#}_{b,n},t^{\#}_{b,n}) \displaystyle G_{\Delta,ren,n}(\phi^{\#}_{a,n},t^{\#}_{a,n};\phi_{b},t_{b}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle G_{\Delta,ren,n}(\phi^{\#}_{a,n-1},t^{\#}_{a,n-1};\phi^{*}_{b,1},t^{*}_{b,1})=G_{\Delta,ren,n}(\phi_{a},t_{a};\phi^{*}_{b,n},t^{*}_{b,n}). $$

In formulae (3.49) and (3.51) we do not specify ranges of summation over $n$ . We clarify ranges of summation for static defect in Sect.3.2 and for moving defect in Sect.3.3. As has been noted in Sect.2.3 the function $G_{\Delta,AdS}(\phi_{a},t_{a};\phi_{b},t_{b})$ is related with the renormalized geodesic lengths. The function $G_{\Delta,ren,n}(\phi^{*}_{a,n},t^{*}_{a,n};\phi_{b},t_{b})$ also is related with renormalized geodesic lengths for the cases when geodesics cross the wedge, see Sect.3.4 Therefore, we can shortly write

$$ \displaystyle G_{l.s.}(\phi_{a},t_{a};\phi_{b},t_{b})=\sum e^{-\Delta{\cal L}_{ren}(\phi_{a},t_{a};\phi_{b},t_{b})}. $$

Here the sum is over all geodesics connecting the points $a$ and $b$ with coordinates $(\phi_{a},t_{a}),(\phi_{b},t_{b})$ that belong to the living space of the $AdS_{3}$ with a wedge. The presence of $\Theta$ -functions is implicitly assumed and summation only over geodesics with $\Theta=1$ is relevant. These geodesic configurations can be different for different points choice and characteristics of moving particles.

In Sect.3.3 we consider representation (3.52) for the $AdS_{3}$ with one moving defect. To make our presentation more clear we start from one static defect, Sect.3.2.

### 3.2 Static defect.

In this section we formulate the renormalized image method of counting and calculation of geodesic contributions in the right hand side of formula (3.52) for the $AdS_{3}$ with one static defect. This case has been considered in the previous papers [29] for spacelike separated points and in [30, 33] for timelike separated points. We start from this case to set the notations and to describe our general method in a simpler case.

#### 3.2.1 Equal-time points.

Now we formulate the image method for the case of one static defect and for equal-time points. Our prescription for calculation gives:

$$ \displaystyle G_{l.s}\left(\phi_{a},t_{a},\phi_{b},t_{a}\right) \displaystyle= \displaystyle G_{\Delta,AdS}\left(\phi_{a},t_{a},\phi_{b},t_{a}\right) \displaystyle+ \displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{n=n_{max}}G_{\Delta,ren,n}\left(\phi_{a},t_{a},\phi_{b^{\star\,n}},t_{a}\right)+\sum_{n=1}^{n=\bar{n}_{max}}G_{\Delta,ren,n}\left(\phi_{a},t_{a},\phi_{b^{\#n}},t_{a}\right). $$

Let us make a few comment about this formula. According to this formula to calculate the correlator we have to take into account:

- • contribution from the basic geodesic connecting points $a$ and $b$ ;

- • contributions from the geodesics connecting $a$ and all imaginary points $b^{\star\,n}$ of $b$ ,

$$ b^{*\,n}\equiv b^{\underbrace{*...*}_{n}} $$

that lie in the right from $a$ half circle, i.e.

$$ |\phi_{a}-\phi_{b^{*\,n}}|<\pi,\,\,\,\,\,n\leq n_{max} $$

(3.54)

- • contributions from the geodesics connecting $A$ and all imaginary points $b^{\#\,n}$ of $b$ ,

$$ b^{\#\,n}=b^{\underbrace{\#...\#}_{n}} $$

lying in the left from $a$ half circle i.e.

$$ |\phi_{a}-\phi_{b^{\#\,n}}|<\pi,\,\,\,\,\,n\leq\bar{n}_{max}. $$

(3.55)

More explicitly our prescription has the form:

$$ \displaystyle G_{l.s.}\left(\phi_{a},t_{a},\phi_{b},t_{a}\right)=G_{\Delta,AdS}\left(\phi_{a},t_{a},\phi_{b},t_{a}\right) \displaystyle+ \displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{n=n_{max}}G_{\Delta,AdS}\left(\phi_{a},t_{a},\phi_{b}+n\bar{\alpha},t_{a}\right)+\sum_{n=1}^{n=\bar{n}_{max}}G_{\Delta,AdS}\left(\phi_{a},t_{a},\phi_{b}-n\bar{\alpha},t_{a}\right), $$

where $\bar{\alpha}=2\pi-\alpha$ , $n_{max}$ and $\bar{n}_{max}$ are given by (3.54) and (3.55). In the case $\alpha<\pi$ we have only one image point and the presence of the contribution of the additional geodesic depends on position of the points $a$ and $b$ , see [30]. For the case $\alpha>\pi$ we can get several terms in (3.56).

In Fig.8.A the contributions of additional geodesics are shown. The geodesics connect the point $a$ with 3 image points obtained by the counterclockwise rotation of the point $b$ on the angle $\bar{\alpha}$ , $2\bar{\alpha}$ and $3\bar{\alpha}$ , respectively. The geodesic $ab^{***}$ does not contribute since $b^{***}$ is out of the right semi circle indicated by the red line. In the Fig.9.A contributions of additional geodesics are shown. The geodesics connect the point $a$ and the imaginary point $b^{\#}$ , obtained by the clockwise rotation on the angle $\bar{\alpha}$ of the point $b$ , can be represented as a sum of two geodesics . One can seen that the geodesics $ab^{\#\#}$ and $ab^{\#\#\#}$ do not contribute since its length corresponds to a connection of the point $a$ with the point $b^{\prime}$ that is not the image of $b$ . #### 3.2.2 Proof of periodicity

To proof that (3.56) defines the correlator on the circle, we have to check that

$$ G_{l.s.}\left(\phi_{a},t_{a},\phi_{b},t_{a}\right)=G_{l.s.}\left(\phi_{a},t_{a},\phi_{b}+\bar{\alpha},t_{a}\right). $$

Let us consider a particular case presented in Fig.10.A. For this case there are the following contributions to the LHS of (3.57): the contribution from the geodesic connecting the points $a$ and $b$ (the basic geodesic), then the contributions from geodesics connecting the point $a$ with the image points $b^{*}$ , $b^{**}$ and $b^{\#}$ , i.e. in (3.54), (3.55) $n_{max}=2$ , $\bar{n}_{max}=1$ .

To calculate the RHS of (3.57) we note that after the shift $\phi_{b}\to\phi_{b}+\bar{\alpha}$ according to our prescription there are the following contributions. There is the contribution from the basic geodesic between points pair $(a,c)$ , here we denote the point with coordinates $(\phi_{b}+\bar{\alpha},t_{a})$ as $c$ (see Fig.10 B). There are also contributions from the image geodesics between points pairs $(a,c^{*})$ that is the same as $(a,b^{**})$ , $(a,c^{\#})$ that is the same as $(a,b)$ and $(a,c^{\#\#})$ that is the same as $(a,b^{\#})$ , i.e. $n_{max}$ and $\bar{n}_{max}$ are changed so that $n_{max}=1$ , $\bar{n}_{max}=2$ (see Fig.10 B). Therefore the changes of $n_{max}$ and $\bar{n}_{max}$ after the shift on the period preserves the set of contributing geodesics, that makes $G_{l.s.}$ periodic.

- • The basic geodesic contributes and the winding one does not.

- • The basic geodesic does not contribute, and the winding one does.

### 3.4 Renormalization

#### 3.4.1 Spacelike geodesics

Now we consider the problem of finding the renormalized length of the image geodesic between two points on the boundary. Consider the geodesic between two near the boundary points $(\phi_{a},t_{a})$ , $(\phi_{b},t_{b})$ that passes through the wedge. It can be represented as a geodesic consisting of two parts (see Fig.14) whose lengths are $l_{a,o^{*}}$ and $l_{o,b}$ . Here point $o^{*}$ is the image of the point $o$ under the isometry (2.12).

The isometry should respects the geodesic length between two points in the bulk i.e. $l_{o,b}=l_{o^{*},b^{*}}$ therefore the length between points $a$ and $b$ must satisfy:

$$ \displaystyle{\mathcal{L}}_{reg}(a,b)={\mathcal{L}}_{reg}(a,b^{*})={\mathcal{L}}_{reg}(a^{\#},b). $$

Here ”reg” means the regularized length. The regularization means, as has been explained above, that we consider points $a$ , $b$ , $a^{\#}$ and $b^{*}$ near the boundary. Expressions for renormalized lengths between points $(a,b^{*})$ and $(a^{\#},b)$ are:

$$ \displaystyle{\mathcal{L}}_{ren}(a,b^{*}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\ln 2[\cos(t_{a}-t^{*}_{b})-\cos(\phi_{a}-\phi^{*}_{b})], \displaystyle{\mathcal{L}}_{ren}(a^{\#},b) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\ln 2[\cos(t^{\#}_{a}-t_{b})-\cos(\phi^{\#}_{a}-\phi_{b})]. $$

It is obvious that these lengths are not equal. Let us do the calculations from the beginning taking into account the divergent part dependence on $\chi$ accurately. We define

$$ \displaystyle{\mathcal{L}}_{ren}(a,b^{*})={\mathcal{L}}_{reg}(a,b^{*})-(\chi_{a}+\chi_{b^{*}}), \displaystyle{\mathcal{L}}_{ren}(a^{\#},b)={\mathcal{L}}_{reg}(a^{\#},b)-(\chi_{a^{\#}}+\chi_{b}). $$

The renormalized geodesic length between points $a$ and $b$ also is:

$$ \displaystyle{\mathcal{L}}_{ren}(a,b) \displaystyle= \displaystyle{\mathcal{L}}_{reg}(a,b)-(\chi_{a}+\chi_{b}). $$

From (3.63) we can write:

$$ \displaystyle{\mathcal{L}}_{ren}(a,b)={\mathcal{L}}_{reg}(a^{\#},b)-(\chi_{a}+\chi_{b})={\mathcal{L}}_{reg}(a,b^{*})-(\chi_{a}+\chi_{b}). $$

Substituting (3.64) in (3.65) we have:

$$ \displaystyle{\mathcal{L}}_{ren}(a^{\#},b) \displaystyle= \displaystyle{\mathcal{L}}_{ren}(a,b)-(\chi_{a^{\#}}+\chi_{b})+\chi_{a}+\chi_{b}={\mathcal{L}}_{ren}(a,b)+\chi_{a}-\chi_{a^{\#}}, \displaystyle{\mathcal{L}}_{ren}(a,b^{*}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle{\mathcal{L}}_{ren}(a,b)-(\chi_{a}+\chi_{b^{*}})+\chi_{a}+\chi_{b}={\mathcal{L}}_{ren}(a,b)+\chi_{b}-\chi_{b^{*}}, $$

and we obtain:

$$ \displaystyle{\mathcal{L}}_{ren}(a^{\#},b)={\mathcal{L}}_{ren}(a,b^{*})+\chi_{a}-\chi_{a^{\#}}-\chi_{b}+\chi_{b^{*}}. $$

According to (2.16) for the large $\chi$ we have:

$$ \displaystyle\chi_{b^{*}} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\chi_{b}+\frac{1}{2}\ln C_{b^{*}},\,\,C_{b^{*}}=\left(\mathcal{B}_{\xi}(\alpha)\cos\phi_{b}+\sin t_{b}(1+2\sinh^{2}\xi\sin^{2}\frac{\alpha}{2})\right)^{2}+\cos^{2}t_{b}, \displaystyle\chi_{a^{\#}} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\chi_{a}+\frac{1}{2}\ln C_{a^{\#}},\,\,C_{a^{\#}}=\left(\mathcal{B}_{\xi}(-\alpha)\cos\phi_{a}+\sin t_{a}(1+2\sinh^{2}\xi\sin^{2}\frac{\alpha}{2})\right)^{2}+\cos^{2}t_{a}, $$

where $\mathcal{B}_{\xi}(\alpha)$ is given by (2.14). Finally, using (3.66) we obtain the renormalized image geodesic length in the case of the removed regularization (for points $a$ and $b$ on the boundary):

$$ \displaystyle{\mathcal{L}}_{ren}(a,b) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\ln[2\left(\cos(t^{\#}_{a}-t_{b})-\cos(\phi^{\#}_{a}-\phi_{b})\right)C_{a^{\#}}^{1/2}] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\ln[2\left(\cos(t_{a}-t^{*}_{b})-\cos(\phi_{a}-\phi^{*}_{b})\right)C_{b^{*}}^{1/2}]. $$

Let us consider the case when the geodesic passes few times through the faces of the wedge and then reach the boundary point forming multiple winding geodesics configuration. This is the case when massive particle deforming the $AdS$ is heavy enough, i.e. $\alpha>\pi$ . In Fig.13 we plot this situation. The geodesics of our interest consists of the pieces $(b,o_{1})$ , $(o_{1}^{*},o_{2})$ and $(o_{2}^{*},a)$ . From the previous section we see, that each image of the point to be renormalized (let’s assume point $a$ ) adds the factor $C_{a^{\#}}^{-1/2}$ for the $\#$ image and $C_{a^{*}}^{-1/2}$ for $*$ . Thus for the two point function for the geodesic connecting $a$ and $b$ as it is show in Fig.13.B. we get the representation for factors $Z_{n}$ and $\bar{Z}_{n}$ for multiple imaging geodesics:

$$ \displaystyle Z_{n}(t^{\#}_{a,n},\phi^{\#}_{a,n};t_{b},\phi_{b}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle C_{a^{\#n}}^{-1/2}=C_{a^{\#(n-1)}}^{-1/2}C_{b^{*}}^{-1/2}=...=C_{b^{*n}}^{-1/2} \displaystyle\bar{Z}_{n}(t^{*}_{a,n},\phi^{*}_{a,n};t_{b},\phi_{b}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle C_{a^{*}}^{-1/2}=C_{a^{*(n-1)}}^{-1/2}C_{b^{\#}}^{-1/2}=...=C_{b^{\#n}}^{-1/2}. $$

#### 3.4.2 Quasigeodesics

In this subsection we will find the renormalized length between timelike separated points ( $a$ and $b$ ). The length between points in the bulk can also be found, as in the previous subsection, using (2.23). In accordance to Fig.15 the length consists of three parts and can be written as:

$$ {\mathcal{L}}(a,b)={\mathcal{L}}(a,h_{1})+{\mathcal{L}}(h_{2},o^{*})+{\mathcal{L}}(o,b). $$

Taking in to account that the length is invariant under the isometry and also that points $o$ and $o^{*}$ are identical we get:

$$ {\mathcal{L}}(o,b)={\mathcal{L}}(o^{*},b^{*}),\,\,\,\,{\mathcal{L}}(a,b)={\mathcal{L}}(a,h_{1})+{\mathcal{L}}(h_{2},b^{*}). $$

*Figure 15: The plot of the quasigeodesic connecting $a$ and $b$ consists from the black curve between points $a^{\#}$ and $b$ and the magenta curve between points $a$ and $b^{*}$ . Here we take parameter values: $\xi=1$ and $\alpha=1$ .*

According to (2.32) we can rewrite the lengths with divergent parts:

$$ \displaystyle{\mathcal{L}}(a,h_{1})={\mathcal{L}}_{ren}(a,h_{1})+\chi_{a},\,\,\,\,{\mathcal{L}}(b^{*},h_{2})={\mathcal{L}}_{ren}(b^{*},h_{2})+\chi_{b^{*}}. $$

Taking into account expression (2.35) for renormalized length we can write:

$$ {\mathcal{L}}(a,b)={\mathcal{L}}(a,b^{*})={\mathcal{L}}(a,h_{1})+{\mathcal{L}}(b^{*},h_{2})={\mathcal{L}}_{ren}(a,b^{*})+\chi_{a}+\chi_{b^{*}}-2\ln 2. $$

On the other hand the formula for length between points $a$ and $b$ has a form:

$$ {\mathcal{L}}(a,b)={\mathcal{L}}_{ren}(a,b)+\chi_{a}+\chi_{b}-2\ln 2. $$

From (3.69) and (3.70) we get the renormalized length for timelike separated points:

$$ \displaystyle{\mathcal{L}}_{ren}(a,b) \displaystyle= \displaystyle{\mathcal{L}}_{ren}(a,b^{*})-(\chi_{b}-\chi_{b^{*}})={\mathcal{L}}_{ren}(a,b^{*})+\frac{1}{2}\ln C_{b^{*}} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\ln[2|\cos(t_{a}-t_{b^{*}})-\cos(\phi_{a}-\phi_{b^{*}})|C_{b^{*}}^{1/2}]. $$

Also by the same way the formula for the renormalized geodesic length can be calculated using $a^{\#}$ and $b$ points:

$$ \displaystyle{\mathcal{L}}_{ren}(a,b) \displaystyle= \displaystyle{\mathcal{L}}_{ren}(a^{\#},b)-(\chi_{a}-\chi_{a^{\#}})={\mathcal{L}}_{ren}(a^{\#},b)+\frac{1}{2}\ln C_{a^{\#}} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\ln[2|\cos(t_{a^{\#}}-t_{b})-\cos(\phi_{a^{\#}}-\phi_{b})|C_{a^{\#}}^{1/2}]. $$

Therefore the formula for renormalization for quasigeodesics is (3.68) again.

## 5 Conclusion

In this paper we have investigated the correlation functions of conformal operators in the theory dual to the $AdS_{3}$ deformed by moving massive particles. Our calculations are based on the geodesic approximation. This approximation works well for operators with large conformal dimension $\Delta$ . However, we have considered how this approximation works starting from $\Delta=1$ . We find, that the 2-point correlation function gets additional contributions due to the nontrivial geodesic structure of the deformed spacetime. The presence of these additional geodesics does not depend on the conformal dimension. The additional geodesics are found via the renormalized image method. In the work we did not take into account the contribution of geodesics between timelike separated points.

We get two different pictures of behaviour of the 2-point correlators on the boundary of $AdS_{3}$ deformed by moving/static particles. The first case, is when the particle deforming the $AdS_{3}$ is light. In this case additional contributions mentioned above give us to the following picture: we have two different zones separated by discontinuity. One of the zones corresponds to the original correlator of the conformal field on the cylinder. Another zone corresponds to the deformed theory, i.e. constant level lines of the inverse correlator are slightly deformed. The second case is the case of the heavy particle. In this case 2-point correlator differs qualitatively: it is deformed in a whole space and there are many different contributions from different multiple winding geodesics. The number of winding depends on the ratio $2\pi/\bar{\alpha}$ , where $\bar{\alpha}$ is the angle of the living space.

It is interesting to compare the results presented in the paper with correlators obtained using the scalar field in the bulk via the GKPW prescription [2, 3]. This is a subject of paper [44]. The image method for timelike separated points and a continuation of correlators to the entire boundary have been considered in the paper [45]
